RuleName: SCCM Software Update Group has been removed
Description: The Software Update Group has been removed in SCCM. Please verify the operation is correct. Removing a group can result in potential vulnerabilities on endpoints.

RuleName: VEBR-001 - Missing Veam Audit Logs
Description: The rule evaluates audit events from the Veeam_BR_CL table to identify a disruption in log delivery from Veeam Backup & Replication to Microsoft Sentinel. It monitors the continuity of log ingestion and triggers when no audit logs have been received within a defined time threshold (configurable) during the specified observation window. Such gaps in audit logging may indicate issues such as network misconfiguration, logging pipeline failure, ingestion delays, or potential malicious activity aimed at suppressing log generation or forwarding. Maintaining consistent log flow is essential to ensure visibility into backup operations and related security events. Alert Records: - Last Log Time: Timestamp of the most recent log received from Veeam Backup & Replication. - Time Since Last Log: Human-readable duration since the last received log. - Time Delta (minutes): Time difference between the current time and the last received log. - Type: Log category or event type associated with the last received record. Monitoring interruptions in Veeam audit log ingestion helps detect potential visibility gaps and ensures the reliability of security monitoring, alerting, and forensic analysis.

RuleName: VEBR-002 - Four-Eyes Activity Monitoring for Veeam Backup
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the Veeam_BR_CL table to identify activities related to the Four-Eyes authorization mechanism in Veeam Backup & Replication. The rule monitors security-relevant operations that require dual control approval, including: Enabling Four-Eyes authorization Disabling Four-Eyes authorization Creation of authorization requests Approval of authorization requests The Four-Eyes authorization feature is designed to reduce the risk of unauthorized or accidental critical actions within the backup infrastructure. These actions may include deletion of backup data, modification of backup repositories, removal of configuration data, or operations affecting Veeam Cloud Connect environments. By requiring approval from another privileged user, this mechanism enforces separation of duties and strengthens operational security. Attackers or malicious insiders may attempt to disable this control or abuse the approval workflow to perform destructive or unauthorized actions. Monitoring these events helps detect potential misuse of administrative privileges or attempts to bypass security safeguards. Alert records: - Time: Timestamp of the activity - Activity: Type of Four-Eyes operation performed - Initiator: User who initiated the action - Approver: User who approved the request (if applicable) - Host Name: System where the activity occurred - Description: Detailed information about the performed action - Severity: Assigned severity based on the activity type Monitoring these activities is critical to ensure that sensitive operations within the backup environment are properly controlled and authorized. This helps protect data integrity, prevent unauthorized modifications, and maintain availability of backup systems.

RuleName: VEBR-003 - MFA Configuration Changes in Veeam Backup
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the Veeam_BR_CL table to identify changes in multi-factor authentication (MFA) configuration within Veeam Backup & Replication. The rule monitors key MFA-related operations, including: - Global MFA enabled or disabled - MFA enabled or disabled for specific user accounts - MFA token revocation (reset) These activities directly impact the security posture of the environment. MFA is a critical control that protects against unauthorized access, even when credentials are compromised. Changes to MFA settings may weaken this protection. Attackers or malicious insiders may attempt to disable MFA or modify its configuration to bypass authentication controls or maintain unauthorized access. Monitoring these events helps detect such attempts. Alert records: - Time: Timestamp of the activity - Operation: Type of MFA-related action performed - Initiator: User who performed the action - Target Account: Affected account (if applicable) - Computer: System where the activity occurred - Description: Details of the change - Severity: Assigned severity Monitoring MFA configuration changes is essential to maintain strong authentication controls and protect access to the backup infrastructure.

RuleName: VEBR-004 - Repeated Invalid MFA Codes in Veeam Backup
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the Veeam_BR_CL table to identify repeated failed MFA code entries in Veeam Backup & Replication. The rule detects user accounts for which invalid MFA codes were entered three or more times within the defined time window. Such activity may indicate user error, unauthorized access attempts, or brute-force activity targeting the backup environment. Alert records: - Start Time: Time of the first failed attempt - End Time: Time of the last failed attempt - User Name and SID: Account for which the MFA code was entered - Host Name: System where the activity was recorded - Count of Attempts: Total number of invalid MFA code entries Monitoring repeated MFA failures helps identify suspicious authentication activity and possible attempts to bypass access controls protecting the backup infrastructure.

RuleName: VEBR-005 - User Blocked After Repeated MFA Failures
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the Veeam_BR_CL table to identify user accounts that were blocked after repeated failed MFA code attempts in Veeam Backup & Replication. Such events indicate that the built-in protection mechanism was triggered due to multiple failed authentication attempts. While this may result from user error, it can also indicate brute-force attempts or unauthorized access using compromised credentials. Alert records: - Start Time: Time of the first failed attempt - End Time: Time of the last failed attempt - User Name: Affected account - SID: Security identifier of the account - Computer: System where the activity was recorded Monitoring these events helps identify potential unauthorized access attempts and ensures that authentication protections are functioning correctly within the backup environment.

RuleName: VEBR-006 - Veeam Backup Console Logon by Break Glass Account
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the Veeam_BR_CL table to identify successful Veeam Backup & Replication console logons performed by accounts listed in the Break Glass Accounts watchlist. The rule detects console launch events initiated by highly privileged emergency accounts. Use of these accounts should be rare and tightly controlled, as they provide elevated access to the backup environment. Attackers or malicious insiders may abuse such accounts to gain administrative access, modify configurations, disable protections, or impact backup and recovery operations. Alert records: - Time: Timestamp of the console logon - Account: User account that launched the console - SID: Security identifier of the account - Computer: System where the console was launched - Description: Details of the event Monitoring these activities is essential because privileged account access to the backup console represents a high-risk action and may indicate unauthorized or emergency access misuse.

RuleName: VEBR-007 - Credential Record Activity on Veeam Backup
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the Veeam_BR_CL table to identify activity related to credential records in Veeam Backup & Replication. The rule monitors operations involving credential records used to access components of the backup infrastructure, including: - Credential record added - Credential record updated - Credential record deleted These events may indicate legitimate administrative activity, but they may also reveal unauthorized changes to stored credentials or attempts to manipulate access to backup components. Alert records: - Time: Timestamp of the activity - Activity: Type of credential record operation - Initiator: User who performed the action - Target: Affected credential record - Target ID: Identifier of the credential record - Property Changed: Modified property, if applicable - Old Value / New Value: Previous and new values, if applicable - Login Type: Type of initiator logon - Computer Monitoring these events is important because changes to credential records can affect access to backup infrastructure and may indicate unauthorized administrative activity.

RuleName: VEBR-008 - Backup Copy Move and Restore in Veeam
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the Veeam_BR_CL table to identify backup copy, move, or restore operations initiated in Veeam Backup & Replication. The rule detects the following operations: - Copy Backup - Move Backup - Restore Session Started These activities may represent legitimate administrative actions, but they can also indicate unauthorized backup handling, data exfiltration, or attempts to access or manipulate protected data. Alert records: - Time: Timestamp of the activity - Activity: Type of operation performed - Initiator: User who initiated the operation Monitoring these operations is important because unauthorized copying, moving, or restoring of backups may affect data confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

RuleName: VEBR-009 - Veeam Backup Deletion Activity
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the Veeam_BR_CL table to identify backup deletion activities in the Veeam Backup & Replication environment. The rule detects operations where backups are deleted, including actions that are approved or require additional approval. Such activity may indicate attempts to remove recovery points before a ransomware attack or to hide malicious actions. Attackers with access to backup infrastructure may delete backups to prevent recovery and increase the impact of an incident. Monitoring this activity helps detect misuse of privileged access and protect recovery capabilities. Alert records: - Time: When the deletion operation occurred - Operation: Type of operation performed - Initiator: The user who initiated the operation and Login type - Approval: Information about approval and approving account - Host: System where the event was generated Monitoring this activity is critical because backup deletion directly impacts the ability to recover from incidents. Early detection helps reduce risk and maintain business continuity.

RuleName: VEBR-010 - Veeam Backup Encryption and Password Modification
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the Veeam_BR_CL table to identify changes to backup encryption settings and encryption password management in the Veeam Backup & Replication environment. It detects activities such as encryption password creation, update, deletion, verification, and modifications to backup job encryption settings. These actions may indicate attempts to weaken backup protection or enable unauthorized access to backup data. Attackers may abuse these changes to disrupt recovery or reduce data protection. Monitoring this activity helps detect misuse of privileged access and protect backup security. Alert records: - Time: When the activity occurred - Activity: Related Veeam activity - Initiator: The user who performed the action - Property: Modified encryption-related property - Object ID: Identifier of the affected object Monitoring this activity is important because unauthorized changes to encryption may weaken backup security and increase the impact of a compromise.

RuleName: Account added and removed from privileged groups
Description: Identifies accounts that are added to privileged group and then quickly removed, which could be a sign of compromise.

RuleName: ADDS-001 - Active Directory Break Glass Account Activity Monitoring
Description: This rule evaluates Windows Security Events from Active Directory Domain Controllers to identify activity involving monitored break glass accounts. The rule detects selected authentication and account management events where the target account, target username, or target SID matches an Active Directory break glass account defined in the BreakGlassAccounts watchlist. The monitored events include successful and failed logons, password reset attempts, user account changes, account lockouts, Kerberos TGT requests, and Kerberos pre-authentication failures. Alert records: - Time when the break glass account activity was observed. - Detected event type and activity description. - Target break glass account and target SID. - Initiating account associated with the activity. - Source workstation, where available. - Domain Controller where the event was logged. Break glass accounts are highly privileged emergency accounts intended for exceptional operational scenarios. Any activity involving these accounts should be reviewed promptly to confirm that the usage was expected, approved, and consistent with emergency access procedures.

RuleName: ADDS-002 - AdminSDHolder Modification in Active Directory
Description: This rule detects any modification to the adminSDHolder object within Active Directory by analyzing SecurityEvent 5136. The adminSDHolder object defines the security descriptor template for all protected accounts and groups (such as Domain Admins and Enterprise Admins) within the domain. Changes to this object’s properties or access control list (ACL) are rare and should always be investigated, as they may result in privilege escalation or weakening of security boundaries. Monitoring adminSDHolder is crucial, as unauthorized modifications can enable persistent elevation of privileges, bypass intended access controls, or facilitate lateral movement within the domain. Alert Records: - Time: Timestamp of the modification - Computer: Domain controller where the change was observed - Initiator: Account name, SID, and type of the user performing the change - ObjectDN: Distinguished Name of the modified adminSDHolder object - Modified Attributes: Attribute names with their previous and new values Review any modification to adminSDHolder immediately. Legitimate changes should be extremely rare and typically only performed by trusted senior administrators during planned change windows.

RuleName: ADDS-003 - AD account with do NOT Expire Password
Description: The rule detects whenever a user account has changed the setting in the User Account Control to Password Never Expires (UAC value %%2089). Set the password to Never Expire for accounts in Active Directory (AD) is not recommended, because it can reduce the security of your system. When the password is set to never expire, users do not have to change their password regularly, which means that if an attacker gains access to the password, they could use it for an indefinite period of time. This could lead to the loss of confidential information and damage to your system. It is recommended to set regular password expiration and enable multi-factor authentication to increase the security of your system.

RuleName: ADDS-004 - Base64 encoded Windows process command-lines
Description: Identifies instances of a base64-encoded PE file header seen in the process command line parameter.

RuleName: ADDS-005 - Bulk Deletion of Directory Service Objects from AD
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the SecurityEvent table (Event ID 5141) to identify instances of bulk deletions of directory service objects in Active Directory. It focuses on specific object classes such as user accounts, computer objects, security groups, organizational units, group policies, and other directory containers. A high number of deletions within a short time frame may indicate a compromised administrative account or a malicious insider attempting to disrupt or cover tracks within the environment. Attackers can exploit elevated permissions to remove large sets of directory objects to impair identity infrastructure, cause denial of service, or erase evidence of prior activity. This behavior is often associated with destructive or evasive techniques. Alert records: - Initiator: The user account responsible for the deletions. - ObjectClass: The type of directory objects deleted (e.g., user, computer, group). - Domain: The Active Directory domain in which the deletions occurred. - DeletedObjects: Total number of objects deleted in a short time period. - ObjectDNs: Distinguished names of the deleted objects. Monitoring large-scale deletions of directory objects is essential for identifying potentially destructive actions and preventing further compromise. Early detection enables rapid response and containment of high-impact threats.
Req. modification: Threshold Set SACL Audit - Everyone for Delete and Delete Child O. on domain or specific OU.

RuleName: ADDS-006 - Active Directory Database Extraction Activity
Description: This rule evaluates Windows Security Events (Event ID 4688) and DeviceProcessEvents from Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) to identify suspicious process executions associated with Active Directory database extraction activity. The rule detects command-line patterns and tools commonly used to access, copy, or extract NTDS.dit and related credential material, including NTDSUtil IFM operations, Esentutl access to NTDS paths, direct NTDS.dit file copy or archival activity, shadow copy based NTDS access, registry hive export on Domain Controllers, DiskShadow activity with NTDS context, and Impacket or secretsdump execution patterns. Alert records: - Time when the suspicious process execution was observed. - Host where the activity occurred. - Whether the host is identified as a known Domain Controller. - Account associated with the suspicious process execution. - Process name or process path related to the detected activity. - Classified Active Directory database extraction technique identified by the rule. - Source telemetry table where the activity was observed. Attackers may attempt to extract NTDS.dit and related registry hives to obtain Active Directory credential material, including password hashes and other sensitive authentication data. Successful extraction may enable offline credential extraction, password cracking, privilege escalation, lateral movement, persistence, or full domain compromise.

RuleName: ADDS-007 - Dumping LSASS Process Into a File
Description: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS). After a user logs on, the system generates and stores a variety of credential materials in LSASS process memory. These credential materials can be harvested by an administrative user or system and used to conduct lateral movement using alternate authentication materials. As well as in-memory techniques, the LSASS process memory can be dumped from the target host and analyzed on a local system. Ref: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/

RuleName: ADDS-008 - Fake computer account created in AD
Description: This query detects domain user accounts creation (event ID 4720) where the username ends with $. Accounts that end with $ are normally domain computer accounts and when they are created the event ID 4741 is generated instead. Ref: https://blog.menasec.net/2019/02/threat-hunting-6-hiding-in-plain-sights.html

RuleName: ADDS-009 - Identify Mango Sandstorm PowerShell Commands
Description: The query below identifies powershell commands used by the threat actor Mango Sandstorm. Reference: https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2022/08/25/mercury-leveraging-log4j-2-vulnerabilities-in-unpatched-systems-to-target-israeli-organizations/

RuleName: ADDS-010 - Local User Account Created on Windows Endpoint
Description: This rule evaluates DeviceEvents from Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) and Windows Security Event logs (Event ID 4720) to detect the creation of local user accounts on Windows endpoints (both servers and workstations). Attackers or malicious insiders may exploit legitimate administrative tools or escalate privileges to create unauthorized local accounts. Such accounts can be used for persistence, bypassing detection, or further system compromise. Monitoring this activity aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1136 - Create Account and is critical for identifying security threats and reducing risks. Alert Records: - Time: When the account creation occurred. - Device: The endpoint's name, type (server or workstation), OS, and IP address. - Initiator: The user or process responsible for creating the account, including their domain, username, and security identifier (SID). - Target: Details of the newly created account, including its username and SID. Monitoring local account creation is critical for detecting potential threats, ensuring accountability, and maintaining secure configurations across the organization’s systems.

RuleName: ADDS-011 - Member Added to Local Group on Windows Endpoint
Description: The rule evaluates DeviceEvents from Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) and Windows Security Event logs to detect when a user account is added to a local group on Windows endpoints (both servers and workstations). Adding accounts to local groups is a critical operation that can indicate misconfigurations or malicious activity. Monitoring this behavior aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1136 - Create Account and T1078 - Valid Accounts, focusing on detecting unauthorized changes in group memberships that could lead to privilege escalation or unauthorized access. - Local groups manage access control on individual devices, and unauthorized changes can lead to policy violations or security breaches. - Adversaries may use such changes to gain elevated privileges, bypass authentication mechanisms, or establish persistence. - Tracking these events improves security monitoring and ensures adherence to organizational access control policies. Alert Records: - Time: When the account addition occurred. - Device: The endpoint's name, type (server or workstation), OS, and IP address. - Initiator: The user or process that performed the action, including their domain, username, and security identifier (SID). - Target: Details of the group and the account added to it, including group name, group SID, target username, and SID. By proactively detecting changes in local group memberships, this rule helps organizations mitigate risks associated with unauthorized privilege escalation and enhance their overall security posture.
Req. modification: req Event ID 4798 - A user's local group membership was enumerated to work OK and DeviceEvents (MDE).

RuleName: ADDS-012 - Member Added to Privileged Group in Active Directory
Description: The rule evaluates events where a member is added to a privileged group in Active Directory. The 'ADCustomPrivilegedGroups' watchlist, containing a list of custom privileged groups, is crucial for accurate detection. The alert records the following event details: - Name and SID of the target user - Name and SID of the event initiator - Name and SID of the privileged group Additionally, the rule employs filters to further refine the results, checking for specific conditions such as well-known local and group SIDs, custom privileged groups, and group names containing variations of 'admin.' Identifying these events is imperative for proactive surveillance and the subsequent enforcement of tailored security protocols within the Active Directory infrastructure.

RuleName: ADDS-013 - Midnight Blizzard - Script payload stored in Registry
Description: This query identifies when a process execution command-line indicates that a registry value is written to allow for later execution a malicious script References: https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/03/04/goldmax-goldfinder-sibot-analyzing-nobelium-malware/

RuleName: ADDS-014 - Midnight Blizzard - suspicious rundll32.exe execution of vbscript
Description: This query idenifies when rundll32.exe executes a specific set of inline VBScript commands References: https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/03/04/goldmax-goldfinder-sibot-analyzing-nobelium-malware/

RuleName: ADDS-015 - MSHTML vulnerability CVE-2021-40444 attack
Description: This query detects attacks that exploit the CVE-2021-40444 MSHTML vulnerability using specially crafted Microsoft Office documents. The detection searches for relevant files used in the attack along with regex matches in commnadline to look for pattern similar to : ".cpl:../../msword.inf" Refrence: https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/09/15/analyzing-attacks-that-exploit-the-mshtml-cve-2021-40444-vulnerability/

RuleName: ADDS-016 - AD Domain Auth Policy Insecure Configuration
Description: This detection rule identifies insecure configurations of Active Directory domain authentication policies following a policy change event (Event ID 4739 and 4713). The rule evaluates resulting policy values against defined security baselines and triggers only when the effective configuration does not meet recommended security standards. It focuses on Domain Password Policy and Kerberos Policy settings that directly impact authentication security. Detected scenarios include: - Minimum password length below recommended threshold - Weak or ineffective account lockout configuration - Excessive password lifetime - Disabled password complexity requirements - Enabled reversible password encryption - Disabled enforcement of user logon restrictions (Kerberos) - Excessive Kerberos ticket lifetimes (user, service, renewal) - Increased clock synchronization tolerance The detection is scoped to Domain Controllers to ensure only authoritative domain-level changes are evaluated, excluding local policy applications on member servers. This rule is designed to identify configurations that increase the risk of credential-based attacks, including password spraying, brute force attacks, offline hash cracking, and Kerberos abuse techniques.

RuleName: ADDS-017 - New AD User or Computer Object Created in Unexpected OU
Description: The rule evaluates Windows Security Event logs (Event ID 5137) to detect the creation of user or computer objects in Active Directory outside of expected organizational units (OUs). Attackers or malicious insiders may attempt to create new AD objects in unexpected OUs to bypass security policies, hide malicious accounts, or establish persistence in the environment. Objects created outside the designated OU structure may not inherit the required Group Policy Objects (GPOs), making them less visible and less protected. Alert records: - Time: When the AD object creation occurred. - Initiator: The account responsible for the creation, including username and SID. - Object: Details of the created object (user or computer), including its name and GUID. - Domain: The domain where the object was created. - Object Path: The distinguished name (DN) and the OU where the object was placed. While this rule highlights potentially suspicious object creation, certain rare administrative activities such as the creation of servers, privileged accounts, or service accounts may also trigger this alert and should be validated as legitimate. Monitoring this event is essential because unauthorized AD objects created in unexpected OUs may lack proper controls, evade detection, or enable adversaries to persist in the environment. This activity represents a deviation from normal administrative practices and therefore poses a security risk.

RuleName: ADDS-018 - New group has been created in AD or Windows Endpoint
Description: The purpose of this rule is to monitor and alert on the creation of new security groups in both Active Directory (AD) and local Windows Endpoints. This ensures the timely identification of potentially unauthorized or unexpected group creation, which could indicate security breaches or misconfigurations. The rule applies to the following environments: - Active Directory domains - Local Windows Endpoints by collencting Event IDs (4727,4731,4754) from Windows Security Event logs. Alert records: - Created Time, - Domain - Initiator and Computer, - Group Type, Group Name, Group SID, Group DN, Group Description Privileged groups are recorded in the watchlist ADCustomPrivilegedGroups.

RuleName: ADDS-019 - New process of Remote Access Software
Description: The rule detects new processes relating to common remote access software utilities (watchlist RemoteAccessSoftware) and record each program that is executed, who the program ran as and the process that started this process. You can correlate this event to other event 4689 by Process ID to determine what the program did while it ran and when it exited.

RuleName: ADDS-020 - Non Domain Controller Active Directory Replication
Description: The rule evaluates potential attempts by non-computer accounts (non-Domain Controllers) to retrieve or synchronize an Active Directory object by leveraging Directory Replication Services (DRS). Typically, a Domain Controller (computer account) would perform these actions in a domain environment. If any of the attributes below are accessed by a non-computer account, an alert is generated: - DS-Replication-Get-Changes - DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All - DS-Replication-Get-Changes-In-Filtered-Set Alert records include: - Time and Date - Account - Host Name - IP Address - Properties More information about Active Directory Replication can be found at: https://threathunterplaybook.com/library/windows/active_directory_replication.html

RuleName: ADDS-021 - Password Reset of Active Directory Privileged Account
Description: This rule detects events when the password of a Privileged Account in Active Directory is reset. The password reset of a Privileged Account is a critical event that should be rare and strictly controlled. Such an action should always be preceded by a formal request, typically in the form of a ticket, to ensure proper authorization and documentation. Unauthorized or unexpected resets can be indicative of potential security breaches or administrative errors, and they require immediate investigation to maintain the integrity and security of the Active Directory environment. Alert records: - Password Last Set - Initiator - Target Account - Domain This rule helps in identifying and alerting administrators to these high-risk events to facilitate prompt and appropriate responses.

RuleName: ADDS-022 - Possible Resource-Based Constrained Delegation Abuse
Description: This query identifies Active Directory computer objects modifications that allow an adversary to abuse the Resource-based constrained delegation. This query checks for event id 5136 that the Object Class field is "computer" and the LDAP Display Name is "msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity" which is an indicator of Resource-based constrained delegation. Ref: https://shenaniganslabs.io/2019/01/28/Wagging-the-Dog.html

RuleName: ADDS-023 - Potential Build Process Compromise
Description: The query looks for source code files being modified immediately after a build process is started. The purpose of this is to look for malicious code injection during the build process. More details: https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/azure-sentinel/monitoring-the-software-supply-chain-with-azure-sentinel/ba-p/2176463

RuleName: ADDS-024 - Potential Fodhelper UAC Bypass
Description: This detection looks for the steps required to conduct a UAC bypass using Fodhelper.exe. By default this detection looks for the setting of the required registry keys and the invoking of the process within 1 hour - this can be tweaked as required.

RuleName: ADDS-025 - Potential Kerberoasting
Description: A service principal name (SPN) is used to uniquely identify a service instance in a Windows environment. Each SPN is usually associated with a service account. Organizations may have used service accounts with weak passwords in their environment. An attacker can try requesting Kerberos ticket-granting service (TGS) service tickets for any SPN from a domain controller (DC) which contains a hash of the Service account. This can then be used for offline cracking. This hunting query looks for accounts that are generating excessive requests to different resources within the last hour compared with the previous 24 hours. Normal users would not make an unusually large number of request within a small time window. This is based on 4769 events which can be very noisy so environment based tweaking might be needed.

RuleName: ADDS-026 - Potential Remote Desktop Tunneling
Description: This rule detects remote desktop authentication attempts with a localhost source address, which can indicate a tunneled login. Ref: https://www.mandiant.com/resources/bypassing-network-restrictions-through-rdp-tunneling

RuleName: ADDS-027 - Potential re-named sdelete usage
Description: This detection looks for command line parameters associated with the use of Sysinternals sdelete (https://docs.microsoft.com/sysinternals/downloads/sdelete) to delete multiple files on a host's C drive. A threat actor may re-name the tool to avoid detection and then use it for destructive attacks on a host.

RuleName: ADDS-028 - Powershell Empire cmdlets seen in command line
Description: This query identifies use of PowerShell Empire's cmdlets within the command line data of the PowerShell process, indicating potential use of the post-exploitation tool.

RuleName: ADDS-029 - Process executed from binary hidden in Base64 encoded file
Description: Encoding malicious software is a technique used to obfuscate files from detection. The first CommandLine component is looking for Python decoding base64. The second CommandLine component is looking for Bash/sh command line base64 decoding. The third one is looking for Ruby decoding base64.

RuleName: ADDS-030 - SDelete Recursive Execution on Windows Host
Description: This rule evaluates Windows Security Events (Event ID 4688) to identify recursive execution of SDelete on Windows hosts. The rule detects process creation events where sdelete.exe, or a command line containing SDelete, is executed with recursive deletion parameters. SDelete is a secure deletion utility that can overwrite deleted files and make data recovery difficult. When used recursively, it may indicate destructive activity, attempted data wiping, or removal of forensic artifacts. Alert records: - Time when SDelete was executed. - Host where the process was observed. - Account associated with the process execution. - SDelete process name and path. - Parent process name and parent process ID. - Command line used for execution. This activity may indicate an attempt to destroy data, prevent recovery, or remove evidence after compromise.

RuleName: ADDS-031 - Security Event log cleared
Description: Checks for event id 1102 which indicates the security event log was cleared. It uses Event Source Name "Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog" to avoid generating false positives from other sources, like AD FS servers for instance.

RuleName: ADDS-032 - Security descriptor modified on AD object
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the SecurityEvent log (Event ID 5136) to detect changes made to the security descriptors of Active Directory objects. It focuses on modifications to the nTSecurityDescriptor attribute, which defines access control for directory objects. The rule compares the old and new values to identify specific access control entries that were added or removed. The detection includes objects such as organizational units, group policies, service accounts, certificate templates, and others that are commonly targeted for unauthorized privilege escalation or persistence. Such modifications can allow adversaries to grant broad access, hide objects, deny administrative control, or weaken auditing. Identifying these changes is critical for detecting abuse of permissions and maintaining the security posture of Active Directory. Alert records: - Time: When the change was made - Object: Distinguished name, object class, and name of the modified item - Initiator: Account name and SID of the user who made the change - Computer: Host where the event occurred - Changed values: Specific access control entries that were added or removed Monitoring this activity supports detection of privilege misuse and helps enforce proper access governance within the domain.

RuleName: ADDS-033 - Security Service Registry ACL Modification
Description: Identifies attempts to modify registry ACL to evade security solutions. In the Solorigate attack, the attackers were found modifying registry permissions so services.exe cannot access the relevant registry keys to start the service. The detection leverages Security Event as well as MDE data to identify when specific security services registry permissions are modified. Only some portions of this detection are related to Solorigate, it also includes coverage for some common tools that perform this activity. Reference on guidance for enabling registry auditing: - https://docs.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/advanced-security-auditing-faq - https://docs.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/appendix-a-security-monitoring-recommendations-for-many-audit-events - https://docs.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/audit-registry - https://docs.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4670 - For the event 4670 to be created the audit policy for the registry must have auditing enabled for Write DAC and/or Write Owner - https://github.com/OTRF/Set-AuditRule - https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.security.accesscontrol.registryrights?view=dotnet-plat-ext-5.0

RuleName: ADDS-034 - Scheduled Task Hide
Description: The rule evaluates audit events from the SecurityEvent table to detect deletion of the SD (Security Descriptor) value from registry keys under the Schedule\\TaskCache\\Tree hive. This specific action is a known technique used by malware to hide scheduled tasks from visibility tools like Task Scheduler and schtasks /query, making detection and analysis more difficult. The registry operation identified by Event ID 4657 with OperationType %%1906 indicates a deletion of a registry value. When this deletion targets the SD value in scheduled task registry paths, it strongly suggests an evasion attempt through task concealment. Alert Records: - TimeGenerated: When the registry operation occurred. - Computer: Host where the deletion was performed. - HostName / HostDomain: Parsed host and domain information from the Computer name. - ObjectName: The registry key path. - ObjectValueName: Name of the registry value that was deleted (should be “SD”). - OperationType / OperationName: Type of registry action performed. - Initiator / InitiatorSID / InitiatorDomain: Identity details of the user or process performing the action. Monitoring this type of activity is essential for detecting stealth techniques used by advanced threats to maintain persistence and evade detection in Active Directory environments.
Req. modification: registry auditing must be enabled for HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\TaskCache\Tree, and the corresponding audit policies must be properly configured.

RuleName: ADDS-035 - Starting or Stopping HealthService to Avoid Detection
Description: This query detects events where an actor is stopping or starting HealthService to disable telemetry collection/detection from the agent. The query requires a SACL to audit for access request to the service.

RuleName: ADDS-036 - Successful remote or local logon to Domain Controller
Description: This query detects sucessfull remote or local logon to Domain Controller. Connecting directly to a domain controller should be very rare. All administration should be done through terminal servers or administration tools. Please verify the reason for the event

RuleName: ADDS-037 - Use Kerberos encryption with DES algorithm
Description: The rule check for uses of DES encryption algorithm. DES is a very weak algorithm and once assigned to an account, it can be used in Kerberos ticket requests, even though it is easily cracked. If the attacker cracks the Kerberos ticket, they can steal the token and compromise the user account. It is recommended to disable DES as an encryption algorithm in the user configuration dialog or in the "msDSSupportedEncryptionTypes" attribute at LDAP level. It has to be disabled in the property of an account by unchecking the box "Use Kerberos DES encryption for this account". References: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/services-hub/health/remediation-steps-ad/remove-the-highly-insecure-des-encryption-from-user-accounts https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/blogs/openspecification/msds-supportedencryptiontypes-episode-1-computer-accounts

RuleName: ADDS-038 - User account Created and Deleted or Enabled and Disabled in short time span
Description: The rule identifies User Account activities outside of normal identity management processes. When a user account is: - Created and then Deleted in 10 minutes (threshold) - Enabled and then Disabled in 10 minutes (threshold) This can be an indication of compromise and an adversary attempting to hide in the noise. Actions could mean a bad actor is trying to avoid detection by creating/enabling accounts, using them, and then deleting/disabling the account.

RuleName: ADDS-039 - Windows Binaries Executed from Non-Default Directory
Description: The query detects Windows binaries, that can be executed from a non-default directory (e.g. C:\Windows\, C:\Windows\System32 etc.). Ref: https://lolbas-project.github.io/

RuleName: ADDS-040 - Windows Built-in Guest Account Modification
Description: The rule evaluates Security Events related to the modification of the built-in Guest account on Windows systems (SID 501). This type of account is therefore often subject to hardening measures. Control will actually depend on the exact hardening rules but the expected state is that built-in guest accounts are always disabled. The rule globally creates 3 types of alerts: - Account activation - Password change or reset - Other account modifications The Alert records: - Operation - Password Last Set - Initiator - Target Account - Domain Monitoring the built-in Guest account is crucial for security because this account is a common target for unauthorized access attempts and malicious activities. By tracking modifications to this account, we can detect and respond to potential security breaches, ensuring that only authorized changes are made and preventing misuse of the account.

RuleName: ADDS-041 - Zinc Actor IOCs files - October 2022
Description: Identifies a match across filename and commandline IOC's related to an actor tracked by Microsoft as Zinc. Reference: https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2022/09/29/zinc-weaponizing-open-source-software/

RuleName: ADDS-042 - Member Added to Sensitive Group in Active Directory
Description: The rule evaluates events where a member is added to a sensitive group in Active Directory. The 'ADCustomPrivilegedGroups' watchlist, containing a list of custom sensitive groups, is crucial for accurate detection. The alert records the following event details: - Name and SID of the target user - Name and SID of the event initiator - Name and SID of the sensitive group Additionally, the rule employs filters to further refine the results, checking for specific conditions such as well-known local and group SIDs, custom sensitive groups, and group names containing variations of finance, HR and other relevant terms. Identifying these events is imperative for proactive surveillance and the subsequent enforcement of tailored security protocols within the Active Directory infrastructure.

RuleName: ADDS-043 - Possible Obfuscation via ACL Deny Entry in AD
Description: The rule evaluates audit events from the SecurityEvent table (Event ID 5136) to detect changes to Active Directory object permissions where Deny access control entries (ACEs) have been added. It specifically targets modifications to the nTSecurityDescriptor attribute that may be used to deliberately suppress visibility of directory objects. These Deny entries commonly affect broad security principals such as Everyone and apply to rights like List Content or Full Control, resulting in objects being excluded from standard administrative views, LDAP queries, or security tooling. The rule is intended to identify attempts to conceal Active Directory objects as part of stealth or persistence mechanisms. This behavior is typically associated with adversaries seeking to hide privileged accounts, backdoor groups, or other unauthorized configurations. Alert Records: - Time: When the directory object was modified. - Object: Name, class, and distinguished name (DN) of the modified AD object. - Access Change: A description of the newly added Deny permission. - Initiator: The user or process making the modification, including SID and domain context. Highlighting these ACL changes enables detection of object-level obfuscation techniques designed to evade detection, bypass security controls, or persist within Active Directory environments.

RuleName: ADDS-044 - Unexpected Primary Group Assignment on AD Object
Description: The rule evaluates audit events from the SecurityEvent table to identify changes to the Primary Group attribute of user (Event ID 4738) or computer (Event ID 4742) objects in Active Directory. The primary group is an attribute stored directly on an account, unlike traditional group memberships which are tracked via group object memberships. This rule flags cases where an object’s primary group is changed to something other than the expected default values (Domain Users for users – ID 513, Domain Computers for computers – ID 515), such as Domain Admins or Enterprise Admins. Such changes are often used as a stealthy method to escalate privileges or hide administrative access, as primary group memberships are not typically reflected in standard group membership queries. This behavior is consistent with techniques used to maintain hidden persistence in Active Directory environments. Alert records: - Time: When the group change occurred. - Target: The object whose primary group was changed, including username and SID. - Initiator: The user who performed the change, including domain and SID. - Primary Group: The new primary group name and its ID. - Computer: The host that processed the change. Monitoring changes to the primary group attribute is essential for detecting hidden privilege escalation and unauthorized group changes that may otherwise go unnoticed in traditional audit mechanisms. This visibility helps uncover potential abuse and maintain integrity in Active Directory environments.

RuleName: ADDS-045 - User Account with Empty UPN in Active Directory
Description: This rule evaluates Windows Security Event logs (Event ID 4720 and 4738) to detect the creation or modification of user accounts without a valid User Principal Name (UPN). These events may occur when a UPN is left empty during account provisioning or intentionally removed during user modifications. Attackers or misconfigured administrative processes may create or alter accounts to exclude UPN values, which can hinder proper authentication, auditability, and directory integration. Such activity may serve as an evasion tactic or indicate identity mismanagement. Monitoring this behavior aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1136 – Create Account, and is crucial for identifying improper account configuration that may allow unauthorized access or reduce traceability. Alert Records: - Time: When the account creation or modification occurred. - Device: The host on which the change was logged. - Initiator: The user or process responsible for the change, including domain, username, SID, and logon ID. - Target: The account that was created or modified, including username, domain, SID, and UPN value. Identifying user accounts without UPNs is essential, as they may bypass controls designed to track or enforce identity-based access across systems

RuleName: ADDS-046 - Group Policy Object Modification in AD
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the SecurityEvent table to identify potentially unauthorized or suspicious modifications of Group Policy Objects (GPOs) within Active Directory environments. The rule analyzes changes at two levels: - File system modifications of GPO templates in SYSVOL (Event ID 4663) - Directory service object changes related to Group Policy (Event IDs 5136 and 5141) Activities are flagged when modifications are observed only at the SYSVOL level without corresponding updates in directory services, which is highly suspicious and may indicate tampering or bypass of proper policy management. Legitimate GPO changes should always involve both layers of synchronization. This monitoring aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1484.001 – Domain Policy Modification and is critical for detecting potential tampering with security settings, lateral movement preparations, or persistence mechanisms by adversaries. Alert Records: - Time: Timestamp of the GPO modification activity - GPO Name and ID: Retrieved from the watchlist - Computer: The domain controller where the activity was logged - Process: The process name initiating the activity - Initiator: Domain and username (SID) of the account that performed the action - GPO Object Details: Including GUID, DN, status (Created/Edited/Deleted), and modified properties - Operation: Type of modification (Write or Delete) - Severity: Determined based on whether directory synchronization was missing Monitoring these activities is crucial for detecting unauthorized changes that could alter domain security policies. Isolated file-level modifications of GPOs without corresponding directory updates are rare and often signify malicious intent.
Req. modification: Watchlist GPO + NTFS auditing on the folder: %SystemRoot%\SYSVOL\domain\Policies.

RuleName: ADDS-047 - Pass The Hash Activity via NTLM Authentication
Description: The rule evaluates SecurityEvent logs (Event ID 4624) and Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) DeviceLogonEvents to identify potential Pass-the-Hash (PtH) activity. It correlates interactive or RDP logons on a source device with subsequent NTLM network logons (LogonType 3) from the same device within a defined correlation window (default 8h). Suspicious behavior is identified when a user (User A) successfully logs on interactively/RDP to a device (SourceHost) and, within the correlation window, the same device initiates an NTLM network logon to a different device (TargetHost) under a different account (User B). This mismatch between the locally authenticated user and the account used for network authentication strongly suggests the use of stolen password hashes. Such behavior may indicate that an attacker has obtained password hashes from a compromised host and is reusing them to authenticate against other systems, enabling lateral movement without needing the plaintext password. Alert records: - Time: When the NTLM authentication occurred. - Source Host: The device from which the NTLM logon originated. - Source IP: IP address of the source host. - Authenticated Account: Account used for the interactive/RDP logon on the source device. - Target Host: The device receiving the NTLM logon. - Target Account: The account being authenticated against on the target device. - Logon Types: Details of both the interactive/RDP logon and the NTLM network logon observed. Monitoring this activity aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1550.002 – Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash and is critical for detecting lateral movement and compromised account usage in Windows environments.
Req. modification: MDE. SecurityEvent ID 4624. whitelist of multihost sources and targets.

RuleName: ADDS-048 - Active Directory SIDHistory Injection
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the SecurityEvent table to identify additions to the sIDHistory attribute in Active Directory. The rule detects Event ID 5136 where the sIDHistory attribute was added. It also checks whether the injected SID matches privileged or otherwise critical security identifiers, such as Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, or the built-in Administrator account. Attackers may abuse SIDHistory injection to assign elevated privileges to an account and gain unauthorized access across the domain or forest. This technique is commonly associated with privilege escalation, persistence, and stealthy abuse of Active Directory trust relationships. Alert records: - Time: Timestamp of the modification - Initiator account details - Target Account details - Injected SID details Monitoring this activity is important because unauthorized SIDHistory changes may allow an attacker to inherit privileged access without being directly added to sensitive groups.

RuleName: ADDS-049 - Active Directory Rogue DC Registration (DCShadow)
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the SecurityEvent table to identify the creation or modification of Active Directory objects related to Domain Controller registration. The rule detects Event ID 5137 and Event ID 5136 with the AddValue operation for objects of class nTDSDSA or server under the CN=Sites container. These events may indicate that a system was registered as a Domain Controller in Active Directory. Such activity is highly uncommon during standard Active Directory operations and may indicate rogue Domain Controller registration or the DCShadow technique, where an attacker registers a temporary Domain Controller to introduce unauthorized directory changes through replication. This may include ACL modification, group membership changes, or SIDHistory manipulation. Alert records: - Time of the last related event - Initiator details - Target details - Modified attributes related to the registration Monitoring this activity is important because unauthorized Domain Controller registration may allow an attacker to replicate malicious directory changes and compromise the integrity of Active Directory.

RuleName: ADDS-050 - LSASS Credential Dumping Activity on Windows Endpoint
Description: TThis rule evaluates Windows Security Events (Event ID 4688) and DeviceProcessEvents from Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) to identify suspicious process executions associated with LSASS credential dumping activity on Windows endpoints. The rule detects known tools and command-line patterns commonly used to access or dump LSASS memory, including Mimikatz, SafetyKatz, ProcDump, NanoDump, PPLDump, LSASSY, PyPyKatz, PowerSploit Out-Minidump, Task Manager dump activity, and rundll32 execution of comsvcs.dll MiniDump functionality. Alert records: - Time when the suspicious process execution was observed. - Windows endpoint where the activity occurred. - Account associated with the suspicious process execution. - Process name, process path, and command line related to the detected activity. - Classified LSASS dumping technique or tool identified by the rule. - Process hash, where available. Attackers may attempt to dump LSASS memory to extract credentials, password hashes, Kerberos tickets, or other authentication material that could be used for privilege escalation, lateral movement, or further compromise.

RuleName: ADDS-051 - KrbRelayUp Local Privilege Escalation
Description: This rule evaluates Windows Security Events from AD Domain Controllers to identify suspicious activity associated with potential KrbRelayUp local privilege escalation. The rule correlates the creation of a new AD computer object with a later addition of sensitive delegation or key credential attributes on a computer object. It monitors Event ID 5137 for computer object creation and Event ID 5136 for added values in msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity or msDS-KeyCredentialLink. Alert records: - Created computer object and target computer object. - Account that created the computer object. - Account that modified the sensitive attribute. - Modified attribute and related technique classification. - Time difference between object creation and attribute modification. - Correlation reason explaining why the events were linked. This activity may indicate preparation or execution of a KrbRelayUp-like privilege escalation chain. Attackers may create or use a machine account and then configure Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) or Shadow Credentials to gain elevated access to a domain-joined computer.

RuleName: Audit policy manipulation using auditpol utility
Description: This detects attempt to manipulate audit policies using auditpol command. This technique was seen in relation to Solorigate attack but the results can indicate potential malicious activity used in different attacks. The process name in each data source is commented out as an adversary could rename it. It is advisable to keep process name commented but if the results show unrelated false positives, users may want to uncomment it. Refer to auditpol syntax: https://docs.microsoft.com/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/auditpol Refer to our M365 blog for details on use during the Solorigate attack: https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/

RuleName: Email access via active sync
Description: This query detects attempts to add attacker devices as allowed IDs for active sync using the Set-CASMailbox command. This technique was seen in relation to Solorigate attack but the results can indicate potential malicious activity used in different attacks. - Note that this query can be changed to use the KQL "has_all" operator, which hasn't yet been documented officially, but will be soon. In short, "has_all" will only match when the referenced field has all strings in the list. - Refer to Set-CASMailbox syntax: https://docs.microsoft.com/powershell/module/exchange/set-casmailbox?view=exchange-ps

RuleName: Exchange OAB Virtual Directory Attribute Containing Potential Webshell
Description: This query uses Windows Event ID 5136 in order to detect potential webshell deployment by exploitation of CVE-2021-27065. This query looks for changes to the InternalHostName or ExternalHostName properties of Exchange OAB Virtual Directory objects in AD Directory Services where the new objects contain potential webshell objects. Ref: https://aka.ms/ExchangeVulns

RuleName: Malware in the recycle bin
Description: The query detects Windows binaries that can be used for executing malware and have been hidden in the recycle bin. The list of these binaries is sourced from https://lolbas-project.github.io/ References: https://azure.microsoft.com/blog/how-azure-security-center-helps-reveal-a-cyberattack/.

RuleName: Service Principal Name (SPN) Assigned to User Account
Description: This query identifies whether a Active Directory user object was assigned a service principal name which could indicate that an adversary is preparing for performing Kerberoasting. This query checks for event id 5136 that the Object Class field is "user" and the LDAP Display Name is "servicePrincipalName". Ref: https://thevivi.net/assets/docs/2019/theVIVI-AD-Security-Workshop_AfricaHackon2019.pdf

RuleName: ZYXL-001 - Missing Zyxel Audit Logs from Network Device
Description: The rule evaluates audit events from the Zyxel_CL table to identify Zyxel devices that have stopped sending log events to Microsoft Sentinel. It analyzes log delivery continuity across all monitored Zyxel systems and flags those that have not sent any logs in the last 120 minutes (configurable threshold) despite activity in the preceding 12-hour observation window. Such gaps in audit logging may indicate potential issues like network misconfiguration, logging service failure, intentional log suppression, or device compromise. Maintaining consistent log flow is critical to ensuring visibility into network security events and supporting incident investigation and compliance efforts. Alert Records: - Device: Name, vendor, product type, and external ID of the Fortinet device. - Time: Timestamp of the last received log from the device. - Time Since Last Log: Human-readable time duration since the last log. - Log Count: Total logs received in the previous 12 hours. - System: Hostname or IP address from which the log was last received. Monitoring for interruptions in Fortinet audit log ingestion helps quickly detect and respond to blind spots in log coverage, ensuring the reliability of detection mechanisms and forensic capabilities.

RuleName: ZYXL-002 - Zyxel Device Firmware Version Change
Description: The rule evaluates audit events from the Zyxel_CL table to detect firmware version changes on Zyxel devices. It identifies and classifies version changes as either an upgrade or downgrade. Firmware downgrades can be a sign of an attempt to exploit older vulnerabilities or bypass newly introduced security mechanisms. Such actions may be initiated by unauthorized administrators or attackers with access to device management. While upgrades are typically legitimate and informational in nature, downgrades pose a potential risk and should be carefully investigated. Alert records: - Time: When the firmware change was initiated. - Device: The name or external ID of the affected device. - Operation: Classification of the event as an "Upgrade" or "Downgrade". - Version Info: Original and new firmware versions involved in the change. Monitoring firmware version changes is critical to ensuring device integrity, preventing rollback attacks, and maintaining a secure network posture. This rule helps surface unexpected or potentially risky firmware activities.

RuleName: ZYXL-003 - Zyxel User Account Management
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the Zyxel_CL table collected via the Zyxel (CEF via AMA) connector to identify user account management activity on Zyxel devices. It detects events where a user account is created, deleted, or modified. Such activity may be legitimate, but it can also indicate unauthorized privileged access, account misuse, or an attempt to establish persistence on the device. Alert records: - Time: When the activity occurred. - Action: The account action performed, such as created, deleted, or changed. - Target account: The administrator username and user type. - Initiator: The account associated with the action. - Source: The originating IP address and derived location. - Device: The Zyxel device name, product, version, and external device ID. Monitoring this activity is important because administrator account changes on network devices can affect privileged access and device security. Early visibility helps identify unauthorized changes and supports timely investigation.

RuleName: ZYXL-004 - Brute-force Activity on Zyxel Device
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the Zyxel_CL table collected through the Zyxel (CEF via AMA) connector to detect brute-force activity against Zyxel devices. The rule identifies multiple failed login attempts against the same account from the same IP address within a defined time window. It also checks whether the failed attempts were followed by a successful login, which may indicate that valid credentials were guessed and used to access the device. Attackers may abuse exposed management interfaces or weak credentials to gain unauthorized access to network devices. Alert records: - Times of events. - Initiator details and IP address and location - Number of failed logins in the time window. - Login method. - Zyxel device name and external ID. Monitoring this activity is important because repeated failed logins, especially when followed by a successful authentication, may indicate unauthorized access to a network device.

RuleName: ZYXL-005 - Zyxel Firewall Configuration Changed
Description: This rule evaluates audit events from the Zyxel_CL table to identify configuration changes on Zyxel firewall devices, including firewall settings, policies, interfaces, NAT rules, access control rules, or other configuration items. These changes may be legitimate administrative actions, but they can also indicate unauthorized activity, misconfiguration, or malicious manipulation of network security controls. Attackers or malicious insiders may attempt to modify firewall configurations to weaken security enforcement, allow unauthorized traffic, expose internal services, disable protections, or create paths for persistence and lateral movement. Monitoring these events helps identify potentially risky changes that could affect the organization’s network security posture. Alert records: - When the configuration change occurred. - The account or entity associated with the configuration change, if available. -The affected configuration type, name, or ID, such as access control, NAT, interface, or policy route. - The IP address from which the activity originated, including whether it is private or public and location. - Zyxel device details, including product, version, external ID, and vendor. Monitoring Zyxel firewall configuration changes is critical for maintaining network security, ensuring accountability, and identifying unauthorized or potentially harmful modifications to perimeter security controls.
